sm: The host, Kato Dal, introduces this episode of Potomac Watch about President Trump's meeting this week with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping on the sidelines of a conference in China, where Trump says nuclear weapons will be a main focus. His guest is Matthew Cronick, who runs a global advisory firm and has written on nuclear strategy. Cronick says Trump is right to seek talks, since there are currently no arms control agreements limiting the superpowers and any future deal must include China as well as Russia. He expects little success, because China has never seriously negotiated and Russia has cheated on past agreements. He says China is on pace for a thousand warheads by 2030 and fifteen hundred by 2035, possibly to support a Taiwan strategy and for prestige.

Cronick agrees Trump was right to let the New START treaty expire, saying it was signed in 2010 and no longer fits today's threats. He describes possible trilateral deals that would serve the United States, such as limits on Russian and Chinese battlefield nuclear weapons, a ban on exotic systems like Russia's nuclear submarine drone and China's orbital bombardment test, or holding China to about 200 weapons. He thinks Putin and Xi will not agree, but that the talks show the world they are the problem. Asked about theater nuclear weapons, he says Russia has about two thousand and an escalate-to-de-escalate strategy, while China has mostly nuclear-capable missiles and a formal no-first-use policy that Pentagon officials doubt. He worries China might use nuclear weapons if a Taiwan invasion went badly.

Cronick says Trump has been interested in arms control since the 1980s, but that history shows breakthroughs come when tensions fall. He believes the world is entering a second Cold War, with years or decades of buildup before reductions become possible. He served on the bipartisan Strategic Posture Commission, which in 2023 recommended the first nuclear buildup since the Cold War because the United States must now deter both Russia and China. That means more than the 1,550 deployed strategic weapons, plus new non-strategic weapons in Europe and Asia, such as the sea-launched nuclear cruise missile. He notes Congress restored that program over Biden administration objections, and he is cautiously optimistic about bipartisan support. The host then raises Trump's Golden Dome missile shield and the argument that it fuels an arms race.

Cronick says leaving the homeland vulnerable makes no sense, since Russia and China are building their own defenses and a shield could blunt limited coercive strikes. He adds that cheap space launch makes space-based sensors and interceptors affordable now. On allies, he says the American nuclear umbrella covers more than thirty treaty allies and is meant to keep them from building their own weapons. A majority of South Koreans favor their own bomb, so Washington should keep reassuring Seoul. He hopes Trump presses Putin and Xi to stop helping Iran, whose targeting data has helped kill American personnel. He says this is unlike Yalta, because this meeting is with adversaries, not victorious allies. Asked about hacking, he says the nuclear arsenal is air gapped and so old it is hard to attack.
